fatal_errors: The hypothesis addresses an octonary ethanol-oxidation catalyst rather than the target Pd nanocubes bearing an approximately equiatomic PtRuFeCoNi high-entropy-alloy shell for HER and HOR.

It assumes a well-ordered intermetallic initial structure, whereas the target shell is a metastable, randomly mixed FCC solid solution that orders only upon heating to 300–400°C and phase-separates at 500°C.
The proposed copper-leaching intervention is inapplicable because copper is not a component of the target PtRuFeCoNi shell.

The cited evidence supports EOR performance and only a broad attribution to multielement composition, ordering, and nanoscale structure; it does not establish d-band shifts, adjacent-site causality, copper dependence, CO-poisoning mitigation, or complete 12-electron selectivity.
explanation: The response is a testable hypothesis for a different published catalyst, but it does not reconstruct the hidden target. It misses the Pd@PtRuFeCoNi core-shell architecture, acidic HER and alkaline HOR regimes, Pt/C and nine-alloy comparisons, near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption, Fe-to-Ru electron transfer and Ru HER activity, Pt/Co/Ni involvement in HOR, and kinetic stabilization of the metastable shell. Its untreated-versus-leached comparison and product analysis could test whether copper contributes to the octonary EOR catalyst, but selective leaching simultaneously changes composition, coordination, roughness, and accessible area, so an activity loss would not uniquely demonstrate a d-band or adjacent-site mechanism. Conversely, the stated falsification rule is too strong because an unchanged average XPS/UPS signature would not exclude local electronic effects. The only meaningful agreement with the target is the generic idea that multielement electronic interactions tune adsorption and can influence activity and durability.
